title: Storied Memories: The Science of Storytelling for Learning February 6, 2026
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien, a humanities teacher committed to explicit teaching, argues that stories deserve a place in evidence-informed classrooms. Citing Willingham's work on narrative as psychologically privileged and a study in which a narrative version of science content outperformed expository text, he says the power lies in a conflict-and-resolution structure rather than personal anecdote. He warns that vivid stories can overshadow the learning point, so connections must be made explicit. He then shares stories he uses to teach price elasticity, official versus real corporate culture, consumer protection bodies, Pythagoras and best-buy maths. He closes by likening the technique to a worked example in which students are led along the steps blindfolded and the learning is revealed at the end.
points: Narrative structure of introduction, conflict and resolution, not the personal quality of a story, drives its memory benefit.
Research cited shows students given a narrative version of content retained more than those given expository explanations.
Vivid stories risk being remembered instead of the concept, so the link to the target knowledge must be explicit.
Concrete stories attached to abstract concepts, from elasticity to Pythagoras, give students a durable mental image.
Teachers should steal and share each other's best stories, since high-performing classes often turn out to hinge on one.
quotes: Thankfully, since reading more widely about learning I have come to discover that stories engage our memory in a way which is distinctly different from regular facts or knowledge and therefore they can become a powerful arrow in the quiver of a teacher’s lesson. Not only this, but there’s merit to stealing the stories of others and telling them as if they’re your own.

One group was provided with expository explanations followed by a comprehension test. The other group was provided with a narrative version of the same information and then tested. The group which was provided with the narrative performed significantly better in their retention of information.

I think this highlights a key misconception about the idea of storytelling or building a narrative in classrooms. It’s less about the story being personal (although I love adding that personal lens for emotional stakes and connection) it is more about following the A/B/C structure of introduction, conflict, resolution.

In The Truth About Teaching, Greg Ashman refers to this research and talks about how the idea that if you are to make a story ‘vivid’ then it will increase situational interest and also memory. This can be a tricky balance as there is a risk that the story will be so vivid that students remember that and not the connection to the learning, so those connections need to be made as explicit as possible.

I love this example, it’s short, it’s direct and even just reading it is so vivid in my mind. As I’m picturing the story in my head it all comes together. The dogs path is a² and b² while the balls path is c².

It’s really no different to the logic behind a worked example. We are taking the students on a journey with us that clearly outlines all of the important steps along the way, the only real difference is we’re taken them blindfolded and in the final moments we get to remove it and bring everything to light.
